title: BANG rescues Ensign Donald E. Corzine, 21–22 April 1945
eyebrow: Sakishima Gunto · BANG's sixth war patrol, lifeguard for the Okinawa campaign

participants.name: Ens. Donald E. Corzine
participants.note: F6F-5 Hellcat, USS CHENANGO; rescued by BANG

paras.text: Hit by flak over Ishigaki airfield on the afternoon of 21 April 1945, a CHENANGO Hellcat pilot spent the night in his raft, fourteen hours by BANG's report, before BANG, already sent from her lifeguard station off Formosa to search for other airmen, took him aboard. BANG's report, his squadron's action report and the Miyako garrison's telegram of the same day, on one GMT clock.

Shot down by medium flak over Ishigaki airfield and ditched about 20 miles east of the island; the other three Hellcats saw him in his raft. BANG had been ordered from her station northeast of Formosa at 1415, before his flight was launched, to search near the Sakishima Gunto for other downed aviators; she reached their reported position at 2330 and, told of him by carrier planes the next morning, took him aboard at 0737. "He had been in the water fourteen hours": neither report times his landing, and fourteen hours before 0737 puts it at about 1737 (assumed). "Replacement clothing was no problem except for his size thirteen shoes."
Ishigaki airfield strike, USS CHENANGO (Air Group 25).

BANG's track runs straight between her reported positions; her search southeast of Ishigaki on the night of the 21st and the pickup itself have no position in her report, so the line doesn't show them. The dashed ring is where the squadron's report puts Corzine's water landing, "about twenty miles East of the Island": an estimate, not a fix. Her 2200 radar-log position (125°14′E as typed) contradicts her own narrative and is drawn dashed.
BANG, CHENANGO's air group and the Miyako garrison all kept zone I (−9), Tokyo time, on 21–22 April 1945, so their local times can be read side by side.

No Japanese record of Corzine's loss has been found. The Miyako-jima Guard Unit's action summary for the 21st (sent 2243) claims one plane shot down and two damaged over Miyako, with no time or place; it is shown for context and is not his. Ishigaki's own report for the day is still missing.

BANG's sixth war patrol report, NARA microfilm M1752 (74802934), narrative pages 11–13 and the Section U radar- intercept log. Air Group 25's aircraft action reports, Report No. 50 (NARA 140031168). The Navy's Nansei Shoto telegram file via JACAR (C19010021200, National Institute for Defense Studies). Coastline: Natural Earth.

events.words: Received orders for lifeguard the next day.
Posit Lat. 24-05N, Long. 122-06E.
Surfaced on lifeguard station. Sky completely overcast with strong wind and rough seas.

Sighted B-24 at about 8 miles on westerly course. He gave no indication of having seen us. No other planes were sighted, and nothing heard on VHF. It seems probable that scheduled strikes were called off on account of weather.
Sighted and exchanged calls with patrolling B-24. He had nothing to report.
Surfaced. Barometer high, but seas still state 5 to 6 from NNE with heavy overcast.
Sighted PB4Y heading southeast.
Posit Lat. 24-34N, Long. 122-47E.
Surfaced. Weather clear and seas moderating.
Received orders to leave present lifeguard station and proceed to point in vicinity of Sakishima Gunto to search for downed aviators. Proceeding at four engine speed.

events.title: Four F6F-5s launched
events.words: Four F6F-5s were launched from the U.S.S. CHENANGO at 1530 "I", 21 April 1945, as a combination strike and Target Combat Air Patrol over Ishigaki Shima. Principal attention was given to the Ishigaki airfield.
events.source: NARA 140031168, ACA Report No. 50, image p248

events.title: Corzine ditches; hit by AA over Ishigaki airfield
events.words: On one of the bombing runs on Ishigaki airfield, Ensign Donald Elmer CORZINE ... received several hits, probably from medium A.A. ... He was able to maintain control over his plane and flew it about twenty-miles East of the Island before being forced to make a water landing. The other three Hellcats circled him ... and ascertained that he was in his life raft.
events.source: NARA 140031168, ACA Report No. 50, image p248
events.note: The report gives no time or position for the landing. The time is BANG's "in the water fourteen hours" counted back from 0737; the position is 20 miles east of Ishigaki airfield. Both estimated.

events.title: The other three return
events.words: Because of the late hour, it was impossible for the Dumbo plane to attempt a rescue that evening. Rescue was effected the following morning by submarine. The other three pilots returned safely to base at 1900 "I".
events.source: NARA 140031168, ACA Report No. 50, image p248

events.words: Southwest of Iriomote Jima encountered strong 156 mc radar interference similar to that encountered by BATFISH on Jap submarine (see section U). Swung ship to determine bearing, but found it to be emanating from the island.

(Section U intercept log, ship position 24°06'N 125°14'E as typed: 156 mc, PRF 500, pulse width 10, antenna rotation irregular; second entry same time and position:) This had the looks of a 103MC carrier modulated with 100% modulation at 350 CPS. It made constant sweeps at 1 R.P.M. Maybe a Jap radar beacon - land based. (As typed, 24-06N 125-14E is about 40 nm south of Miyako Jima, not southwest of Iriomote Jima as the narrative says at 2150. It does fit the run from the 21 Apr noon position at four-engine speed (about 135 nm east in 7.6 h); unresolved.)

Action summary for the 21st. On the 21st, carrier planes (fighters and bombers combined), 83 sorties in all, in formations of 8 to 10-odd, strafed and bombed the Army and Navy airfields in four waves. From 0455 to 0645, B-24s, 2 to 4 at a time, patrolled overhead, strafing and bombing, for about two hours or more; at 0510 one B-24 bombed the airfield; from 1100, two of them circled overhead for an hour and a half, mainly reconnoitring. Results: one shot down, two damaged. No damage to us.
events.original: 二十一日戦闘概報 二十一日来襲艦上機戦爆聯合延八三機八乃至十数機ノ編隊ニテ四次ニ亘リ陸海軍飛行場銃爆撃自〇四五五至〇六四五B二四二機乃至四機ニテ上空哨戒銃爆撃在空時間概ネ二時間以上〇五一〇B二四一機飛行場爆撃同二機一一〇〇ヨリ一時間半ニ亘リ上空ヲ廻リ主トシテ偵察 戦果撃墜一 撃破二 被害ナシ
events.translation: Action summary for the 21st. On the 21st, carrier planes (fighters and bombers combined), 83 sorties in all, in formations of 8 to 10-odd, strafed and bombed the Army and Navy airfields in four waves. From 0455 to 0645, B-24s, 2 to 4 at a time, patrolled overhead, strafing and bombing, for about two hours or more; at 0510 one B-24 bombed the airfield; from 1100, two of them circled overhead for an hour and a half, mainly reconnoitring. Results: one shot down, two damaged. No damage to us.
events.note: Time is the telegram's origination (機密第二一二二四三番電, 21st 2243), not of any action. Telegram from the Miyako-jima Guard Unit (宮古島警, sender) to Sasebo Naval District and Okinawa Base Force (佐鎮・沖根), info Ishigaki-jima Guard Unit (石垣島警); originator's number 機密第二一二二四三番電 (21st 2243), received 22 Apr 0047, decoded 0530-0720; in the Navy's Nansei Shoto telegram file (電報綴 南西諸島 其の4, part 1, page stamped 0879). CONTEXT ONLY, NOT A MATCH: this is Miyako's report, while ENS Corzine (CHENANGO VF) was hit by AA over Ishigaki airfield in a strike launched 1530 I and ditched ~20 mi east of Ishigaki (US ACA Report 50, NARA 140031168 p248); Miyako's 'one shot down' is some other aircraft or claim. Doubtful readings: 延八三機 (83 sorties) has a contemporary pencil '?' beside 三; '一時間半' has a pencil '?' beside 一; it is not clear from the wording whether 自〇四五五至〇六四五 belongs to the carrier strikes or to the B-24s (read here with the B-24s). No time for the shoot-down is given. Ishigaki-jima's own report for 21 Apr was not found in this file or in part 2 (C19010021300 pp. 1-24).

events.words: Arrived at reported position of downed aviators and commenced search southeast of Ishigaki Jima.
Began feeling distant explosions and seeing occasional flashes, presumed to be carrier planes striking Ishigaki Jima and Miyako Jima.

Began making contact with carrier planes. Requested information on any downed aviators and after a brief flurry of communications learned that we were within 20 miles of a downed Hellcat pilot in rubber boat. Planes furnished cover and guided us in.

Took aboard Ensign Donald E. Corzine, file #382983, U.S.S. CHENANGO Hellcat pilot. He had been in the water fourteen hours but was in excellent condition and very glad to be aboard. Replacement clothing was no problem except for his size thirteen shoes. ... this rescue did more for the morale of the crew than anything else could have done with the exception of sinking ships. Every officer and man is proud to have been of some help to those who are now the ball carriers. (No position or cause of loss given. Fourteen hours before 0737 I puts him in the water about 1737 I on 21 Apr.)
Proceeding with search for downed aviators previously reported in our orders.
Released fighter cover. Thereafter during the day numerous planes were contacted, mostly flying high enroute to or from their carriers.
Posit Lat. 24-03N, Long. 124-16E.
(Section U intercept log, ship position 24°01'N 124°12'E: 104 mc, PRF 350, pulse width very wide, antenna rotation 1.) The full scale sweep is as seen in the sketch. Made regular sweeps.

Completed search of probable southern sector. Dove and headed north, intending to transit the channel to eastward of Ishigaki Jima immediately after dark and continue search to northward. Strong northerly winds yesterday would have driven survivors to southwest, but with moderation of weather the northerly current would have taken charge.
Surfaced.

Received orders to return to our assigned lifeguard station to the northeast of Formosa. Proceeding westward. Learned later that the survivors for whom we had been searching had been picked up by a PBM.
Submerged on station.
Sighted unidentified single engine fighter plane on westerly course.
Posit Lat. 24-40N, Long. 122-37E.
(Section U intercept log, ship position 24°20'N 122°32'E:) Same intercepts as 2230, 13 April. 0400, 18 April.
Dove for SJ contact at 4000 yds, moving in fast, nothing in sight. Suspected a plane, although APR had indicated no radars other than the customary assorted land-based air search equipment.
(Section U intercept log, ship position 24°38'N 122°27'E: 155 mc, came on suddenly.) A plane contact was made on the SJ shortly after this intercept was made.

Surfaced; all clear. During remainder of night we made numerous other close-in contacts, moving at various speeds. A check for phantoms ... showed they were real pips. ... My only explanation is that they possibly were porpoises or blackfish, of which a large number were seen during the daytime.
